489.history: Seann-Dhaoine' river harbour on the Abhainn naomh, with a mole and a tower at its mouth. The hill-folk of the upper river were saying its old name before any of them had seen it, in the year Beathan was born. In the six hundred and twenty-eighth year Iain mac Fhearchair brought eleven souls of his household down the river to the empty harbour, marked the ground, and forbade the tower; the household used Seann-Dhaoine' mole as it found it, and when a winter storm broke the mole's oldest stretch Iain would not build with the broken stone. His daughter Marsaili held the household after him, went out in the first hide boats the harbour had held since Seann-Dhaoine, and chose how a household newly of the sea should bury the first one the sea took.
489.known_for: the mole, the tower, and Marsaili's boats

170.history: Tràigh an t-Salainn of the south, where the salt-folk scraped the flats and dried the crust on the shingle. In the six hundred and seventy-second year Mòrag Chruaidh came down on it with eleven spears and took salt, losing seven of her own, whose names the hill kept at its fire. In the six hundred and eighty-third year they made shallow clay basins behind the shingle bar, the first salt-works of the island, and raised a bank behind the pans. Iain Dubh came down in the seven hundred and twenty-seventh year at dawn with more spears, and Tadhg Garbh's spear killed him on the clay. The next summer the king walked south alone; the salt-folk raised spears against him and lowered them, and old Mòr knelt on the wet shingle and gave him a double handful of salt, and from that day the shore was called the king's. The salt-folk built a cairn of their own with seven stones in it, and in the fosterling's day An Cnoc Ruadh's own salt refrain was sung at their pans in words An Cnoc Ruadh itself could no longer construe.
170.known_for: the salt-pans and the double handful

324.history: An old oak grove on the south-west coast. In the seven hundred and fifth year pots of coiled clay, fired in open bonfires in the lee of the oaks, were first made here, and two of the first of them reached Dùn ìseal within the season. Within a few lifetimes the whole southern shore used them, and pots were among the first goods that strangers to both hills set out beside the wool and salt at the ford. The potters dug their clay from the same bank for generations and traded their wares down the drovers' roads.

2004.history: A village of low houses on the south coast under a narrow hill, where the sea rose past every mark it had kept in the seven hundred and seventy-seventh year and came in over the houses in the night, taking twelve of the shore's people and leaving a hand's depth of grey sand over every hearth it did not carry away. Seasaidh, seven years old, was carried up the slope by her mother; her father was among the twelve. The survivors rebuilt higher on the slope and left the old ground unbuilt, and when a lesser wave came in the three thousand eight hundred and seventeenth year it found only empty byres below the new houses. The measure of the full hand was ground into a stone cup here, despite two false starts, in Oighrig's keeping.
2004.known_for: the wave, and the houses on the slope

2002.history: A green valley walled by low scarps two days inland from the coast, where Seasaidh came as a bride with Pàl, a drover's son. In the eight hundred and twenty-seventh year the ground opened below Pàl's byre, a crack that ran along the valley and moved its spring to a new channel. The king walked the length of the crack and forbade nothing. Twenty years later Seasaidh, in her old age, carried white stones up from the stream bed and set them a stride back from the crack's edge, choosing them for their whiteness so a child running in poor light might see where the safe ground ended; the valley finished the line after her, and no house was raised within a stone's throw of the crack. In the three thousand eight hundred and sixty-third year the crack moved again and the spring shifted back uphill and broke the line in two places, and the households laid it again exactly as their grandmothers had.
2002.known_for: the crack and the white stones

15.history: A fishing strait on the southern coast named for the red rock that watches it. Its fishers took to tying woven buoys over the deep channels where the current ran hardest, a custom that spread along the coast in carriers' mouths as the paired tide-marks had spread before it. The settlement was taken up in earnest in the two thousand five hundred and seventieth year, and it traded with the harbour of Seann Skell and the marsh settlement at Muileann naomh. Its households kept the sharing before the storms along the whole strait, and in A' Ghaoth Dhubh's winter sent dried fish north along the coast road with the grain from the valleys.
